[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Database Design: Normalization (1NF through BCNF)"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Database normalization is the systematic approach of decomposing tables to eliminate data redundancy and undesirable characteristics like Insertion, Update, and Deletion anomalies. This tutorial covers normal forms from the First Normal Form (1NF) up to the Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF)."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"First Normal Form (1NF)"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"A relation is in First Normal Form if the domain of each attribute contains only atomic (indivisible) values, and the value of each attribute in a tuple contains a single value from that domain. It also requires eliminating repeating groups."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Ensure each column contains atomic, indivisible values."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Remove repeating groups into separate tables."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Ensure a primary key is defined to uniquely identify each row."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Second Normal Form (2NF)"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"A relation is in Second Normal Form if it is in 1NF and every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on the primary key. This means there must be no partial dependencies, where a non-key attribute depends on only a part of a composite primary key."},{"order":10,"type":"code","text":"CREATE TABLE OrderItems (
    OrderID INT,
    ItemID INT,
    Quantity INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (OrderID, ItemID)
);"},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"Third Normal Form (3NF)"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"A relation is in Third Normal Form if it is in 2NF and every non-prime attribute is non-transitively dependent on the primary key. In other words, all non-key attributes must depend directly on the primary key, not on other non-key attributes."},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Must be in 2NF."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"No transitive dependencies (X -> Y and Y -> Z implies X -> Z)."},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF)"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"Boyce-Codd Normal Form is a stricter version of 3NF. A relation is in BCNF if and only if every determinant is a super key. This means that whenever a functional dependency X -> Y holds, X must be a super key of the relation."},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"-- Example violating BCNF:
-- StudentID, Course -> Instructor
-- Instructor -> Course (Instructor determines course, but Instructor is not a key)"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"By following these normalization steps iteratively, database designers can ensure minimal data redundancy, improved query integrity, and robust schema architecture."}]
